en: A Compendium of the Essential Meaning of the Mahāyāna Sūtras, in One Volume.
Homage to all the unsurpassed Buddhas, Who have realized the three bodies, Honored Ones among gods and humans;
To the Dharma, profound and inconceivable in its teaching; And to the Saṅgha of the unconditioned, in harmonious union.

This is the true refuge in the Triple Gem; the appearance of the Buddhas in the world is as rare as the udumbara flower, or like a blind turtle encountering a floating log. A human body is difficult to obtain and exceedingly rare;
once lost from this point on, it will be hard to expect again. Within this very body, one must gradually advance toward the goal.
Forever and always abandon the eight difficult conditions; Relying on the teachings, practice with increased diligence.
The karma of good and evil does not perish; Just as a seed meets with conditions, so too is the fruit.
Therefore, stay far removed from the ten unwholesome actions, And diligently cultivate the ten wholesome ones.
One must skillfully discern the two truths; constantly renouncing saṃsāra, seek liberation and diligently practice the right path to increase wisdom.
Vowing to cultivate the traces of the sages and realize the unconditioned—thus, all sentient beings must first take refuge in the Triple Gem, reverently serving and looking up to them.
What are the Three Jewels?
They are the Jewels of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
Regarding the Jewel of the Buddha:
That which is called the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body, fully possessing these three, is named the Buddha Jewel.
As for the Dharma-body,
it possesses inconceivable non-conceptual wisdom.
One observes all phenomena with sovereign mastery.
What is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) is the accomplishment of inconceivable merit.
Surpassing the pleasures of humans and devas,
endowed with the marks and signs of excellence, transcending birth and death,
one realizes the ultimate body of Vairocana.
Regarding the "Transformation Body" (nirmāṇakāya):
having brought to ultimate fulfillment his vows of compassion,
he liberates sentient beings throughout the entirety of birth and death.
He spontaneously guided the way, forever departing from all suffering;
he entered the mother’s womb and was born into the world;
he left the household life and subdued the hosts of Māra and his enemies.
He turns the wheel of the true Dharma and manifests the signs of nirvana;
he is one who is fully endowed with all virtues.
It appears only after a period exceeding that of humans and devas;
therefore, it is difficult to encounter.
There is nothing in the world that can serve as its metaphor.
Therefore, by employing worldly treasures to manifest the meaning of the Dharma,
he causes all sentient beings to attain the unsurpassed fruit and forever leave behind the suffering of birth, old age, and saṃsāra.
By taking refuge even in part, one receives protection;
malevolent spirits and ghosts cannot harass or disturb them.
These are the five meanings possessed [by this refuge].
Having obtained the wish-fulfilling jewel, he serves as the teacher of gods and humans for both the mundane and supramundane realms;
because he is the most honored among two-legged beings and the true refuge,
that which is called the "Dharma Jewel" is [defined as follows].
All the teachings are explained in terms of the twelve divisions according to the two truths, the conventional and the ultimate.
By practicing the Eightfold Noble Path, one awakens to the true nature,
which is primordially quiescent and the non-abiding nirvana.
These are designated as the Three Jewels.
Therefore, before the Buddha appeared in the world, his secret and essential Dharma could not be revealed.
The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is exceedingly rare.
The Dharma taught is likewise so;
no other non-Buddhist paths can reveal its meaning,
for all other phenomena cannot equal it.
Because this path of benefit and happiness through the treasure of the Dharma is no different from that of the Buddha,
it is called the Treasure of the Dharma.
As for what is called the Sangha:
The assembly of great bodhisattvas does not cling to saṃsāra nor abide in nirvāṇa;
they have fully accomplished the benefit of both themselves and others.
Furthermore, the various Arhats and the eight classes of noble persons dwell on the ground of liberation;
ordinary bhikṣus each believe and accept [the teaching], delighting in the state of the noble ones as they leave the household life to study the Path.
Through the Pratimokṣa, one practices in accordance with the teachings;
although the fruit has not yet been realized, one is able to practice according to the prescribed rules of conduct.
Even if a Buddha were not to appear in the world, the Noble Dharma and the Jewel of the Sangha would still exist;
they are identical to the rare and marvelous signs manifested by the Tathāgata’s birth,
being fully endowed with all unsurpassed wisdom and virtue.
Based on hearing, reflection, and cultivation, the wholesome gradually becomes subtle.
The various worldlings who are seers and possess noble wisdom cultivate the ground of peace and bliss.
Thus, the creation of the Saṅgha-ratna is supreme.
As with the aforementioned Three Jewels, the power of their various merits possesses great compassion;
they are most honored, most excellent, and inconceivable.
It can uproot the present sufferings and hardships of sentient beings,
causing them to forever leave behind the long kalpas of saṃsāric transmigration;
it can also provide protection so that they may attain the bliss of liberation.
One should make offerings to the unsurpassed Triple Gem.
First, one must reverently prostrate and take refuge in that which gives rise to the sprouts of all merit and virtue,
thereby forever departing from all matters of suffering and affliction.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are endowed with these merits;
their appearance in the world is exceedingly rare,
and they plant roots of goodness together with all living beings.
The appearance of a Buddha in the world is like that of the udumbara flower;
the transmission of the profound Dharma by the Buddhas appearing in the world is likewise.
Although a Buddha appears in the world and there exists this profound Dharma, those who encounter it as human beings must necessarily be endowed with the fulfillment of wholesome karma.
The difficulty is likewise so.
For example, suppose there were a blind turtle in the depths of the great ocean,
with a lifespan of hundreds of millions of kalpas, and it would surface once every hundred years.
Once, having risen upon the water,
suppose there were a person who cast a log with a single hollow into the ocean;
it would be extremely rare for that turtle to surface and have its head meet the hollow of that floating log.
The difficulty of obtaining a human body is likewise so.
Although one may obtain a human body with all six sense faculties intact and hear the True Dharma with both body and mind at ease,
it is most exceedingly rare to practice according to the teachings.
The realm of sentient beings is inconceivable.
Among them, to obtain a human body with its six sense faculties complete and to take birth with mastery is exceedingly difficult.
For this reason, the appearance of a Tathāgata and the manifestation of the Dharma in the world are likewise rare to encounter.
A human body is difficult to obtain;
having now attained this great lot of retribution,
it appears before us only once in time, for it is only through the merit accumulated over many kalpas that one finally obtains a human body.
One must especially apply oneself with diligence so as not to let this spiritual power be abandoned;

one should increase wisdom, the Dharma, and roots of goodness. From this sacred ground onward, one must seek superior practice, vowing never again to fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.

Not hearing the Three Jewels, being born in the borderlands, the lower realms, or among the lowly; though having obtained a human body, being blind, deaf, mute, or dumb; the long-lived heavens; difficulties regarding birth as a human;
or falling into wrong views—these constitute the eight difficulties even when a Buddha has appeared in the world, or during the periods before or after a Buddha’s presence.
They will no longer fall into various states of suffering and affliction that obstruct the Path,
but will forever be free from the eight difficulties;
they shall realize the great fruition of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One.
All practitioners who apply themselves with diligent vigor, as if their heads were on fire, shall eliminate the eight difficulties and achieve great goodness;
yet, not even a hair’s breadth of good or evil karma will perish.
For example, in the past, the rishi Kātyāyana and others, having pricked a deer-fly with a blade of grass on its path,
received the retribution of wooden skewers for five hundred years within their lower bodies.
Later, he died. In the past, there was a youth who, with a mind of reverence, offered a handful of white stone to the Sangha.
By virtue of this causal connection, for immeasurable kalpas he was born into families of great wealth and nobility.
They rain down the seven treasures, fully accomplishing happiness and sovereignty.
According to their virtuous or non-virtuous karma, they receive bodies and the fruits of suffering or pleasure corresponding to their kind.
Since the maturation of karma follows this principle, one must not associate with the ten non-virtuous actions and the like, but must instead distance oneself from them as a matter of course.
What need is there for further words?
As for the ten unwholesome actions, there are three types of bodily conduct: killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
There are four types of verbal [action]:
false speech, frivolous talk, harsh speech, and double-tongued speech.
There are three types of mental [action].
These are greed, hatred, and delusion.
Summarized in this way, they are called the ten non-virtuous actions.
By virtue of their retribution, one is born into the three miserable realms.
The ability to turn away from the ten non-virtues is called the ten virtues.
By abstaining from killing and other such conditions for the ten non-virtues, one will be reborn in the heavens as well as among humans in superior realms.
From this point onward, since one has attained the noble stages, if one is able to practice, all shall be accomplished.
You should know that one who diligently practices the ten wholesome paths among humans and understands the characteristics of all phenomena is called a "great man" (puruṣa).
One is well able to weigh and compare the two truths—the ultimate and the conventional—to realize the principle of the two natures, self and other.
Among these, the phenomena of the conventional truth arise from causes and conditions;
they are like illusions, transformations, dreams, mirages, and heat-mirages.
The elements (*dhātu*) and sense bases (*āyatana*) are categorized as wholesome or unwholesome, meritorious or non-meritorious, mundane or supramundane;
they are distinguished by various characteristics and appearances.
Yet, all these phenomena are merely manifested and expressed through provisional verbal designations.
All contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) naturally have impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self as their characteristics.

As for what are called uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*), they are likewise characterized by emptiness and non-self; thus, through these two truths, one knows the turning of the wheel of all dharmas.

Ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, and old age and death—these twelve links of dependent origination revolve like a wheel through the six realms of existence, giving rise to suffering and providing warmth for the body.
Each attains accomplishment according to their respective faculties, whether sharp or dull, and in accordance with their kind.
That which is called "liberation," the ground upon which the noble ones rely—
those of dull faculty receive the Śrāvaka-yāna.
Those of middling faculties attain the fruit of a pratyekabuddha.
According to their respective faculties, the realizations they achieve differ;
these, together with the unsurpassed Mahāyāna, constitute the three types.
Those of dull faculties realize the Lesser Vehicle;
they are able only to benefit themselves and lack the capacity to benefit others.
Disgusted by the suffering of birth and death, they cultivate the bliss of quiescent extinction.
Abandoning all unwholesome things, as well as the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses,
one first contemplates the Four Noble Truths and practices to realize the stages of the Stream-enterer and the Eightfold Assembly, attaining Nirvana without remainder. As for the Pratyekabuddha,
by contemplating that the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths arise through causes and conditions, they subsequently extinguish the source of birth and death.
Having realized the noble path and *nirvāṇa* without remainder,
they possess the superior wisdom that does not differentiate between the cycle of birth-and-death and *nirvāṇa* as they proceed toward the Great Vehicle;
this is the unsurpassed enlightenment consisting of both self-benefit and the benefit of others.
The Bodhisattva cultivates the dharmas that assist the path through great compassion;
proceeding from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma,
they practice in successive order and realize the state of a Bodhisattva.

Having continued to cultivate the six perfections—the four means of integration consisting of giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation—one becomes fully endowed with merit and wisdom, thereby accomplishing inconceivable, unsurpassed, supreme knowledge.
Having attained the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, they are fully accomplished;
they realize the stage of Buddhahood to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings,
and until the end of the limits of birth and death, they do not enter parinirvāṇa.
A Compendium of the Essential Meaning of the Mahāyāna, One Scroll.
